summaries.example: Imagine a glass of water. You can say “one glass,” but you usually do not say “one water.” If you pour the water into two cups, it is still water. Now compare a toy car: if you cut it in half, you do not have two toy cars. This helps show the difference between stuff, which we measure, and things, which we count.
summaries.summary: This entry studies the difference between stuff and things. Water, iron, and sand are examples of stuff: we often measure them. A dog, a chair, or a rock is a thing: we usually count it. The difference appears in language too. We say “five horses,” but normally say “some water” or “a bottle of water.” Philosophers disagree about what this means. Some think stuff is really a collection or sum of tiny things. Some think it is a set or a group of many things. Others think stuff is a basic part of reality that cannot be reduced to objects. The entry also warns that grammar may not tell us exactly what exists. A word can sometimes be used in both a mass way and a count way, and different languages organize these ideas differently.
key_ideas: We often measure stuff but count things.
Philosophers ask whether stuff is really different from things or is made from things.
Some theories say mass expressions refer to collections or sums of small things.
Other theories say stuff is more basic than ordinary objects.
Words do not always settle the question, because languages use mass and count words in different ways.
summaries.why_it_matters: This topic connects everyday words with big questions about reality. It asks what makes something one object, what parts and wholes are, and how things can change while remaining the same. It also teaches a useful lesson: language gives clues about how we think, but those clues may not be a complete map of the world.

important_terms.definition: Material or non-material substance that is usually measured rather than counted, such as water, wood, or butter.
An individual object that can usually be counted as one, such as a car, dog, or rock.
A word or phrase used for stuff, such as “water” or “the gold in the ring.”
A word or phrase used for countable objects, such as “three dogs” or “one rock.”
The idea that everything real is either a thing or can be explained as things.

questions_to_think_about: Is a puddle one thing, some water, or both?
If you divide water into smaller drops, do you still have the same water?
Why can we count apples but usually measure applesauce?
Can the words we use prove what the world is really made of?

summaries.example: Consider the gold in a ring. A sum theorist may say that this gold is a mereological sum: a whole made from all the relevant gold particles, whether they are in one ring or scattered. A set theorist may identify the gold with a set of gold particles. A pluralist may say that “the gold” refers directly to many particles without referring to one additional object. A stuff ontologist may instead argue that the gold is a genuine stuff entity, not reducible to objects. Each account must explain why the gold can persist through changes that affect the ring, and why ordinary language refers to it as “the gold.”
summaries.summary: The entry investigates what nominal concrete mass expressions—phrases such as “the water in the tub” or “the gold in the ring”—refer to. Its starting point is a familiar contrast: things such as horses and chairs are ordinarily counted, while stuff such as water and iron is ordinarily measured. Thing Theory treats reality as consisting entirely of objects or entities reducible to objects. Against this, stuff ontologies give non-object-like stuff a fundamental role. The main theories that remain compatible with Thing Theory analyze mass reference in three ways. A sum theory identifies a portion of stuff with a mereological fusion of particles or smaller portions. A set theory identifies it with a set of material constituents. A plural theory treats mass expressions as referring to many things without adding a single sum or set. Each proposal faces difficulties involving persistence, coincidence, atomless or indefinitely divisible matter, and vague boundaries. More radical views regard stuff as fundamental and ordinary objects as derivative or conceptually imposed. The final methodological lesson is cautious: mass/count grammar offers important evidence, but it may not justify a full metaphysics. Expressions can shift between mass and count uses, languages differ in their grammatical patterns, and similar linguistic behavior does not always reflect the same kind of entity.
key_ideas: The stuff/thing debate concerns both ontology, the study of what exists, and philosophy of language.
Mass expressions behave differently from count expressions, but the linguistic contrast does not map neatly onto all metaphysical categories.
Three conservative approaches analyze stuff in terms of sums, sets, or plural reference.
More radical stuff ontologies treat stuff as fundamental, or treat ordinary objects as derivative appearances of underlying stuff.
Questions about composition, persistence, and coincidence arise when the same matter constitutes different objects over time.
Mass/count usage varies with context and across languages, so linguistic evidence may underdetermine metaphysical conclusions.
summaries.why_it_matters: The debate tests how far ordinary language can guide theories about reality. It clarifies disputes about parts and wholes, identity through change, and the relation between an object and the matter that constitutes it. It also shows why philosophers must distinguish descriptive questions—how people speak—from metaphysical questions about what fundamentally exists. Linguistic evidence can motivate theories, but it may be too variable and context-dependent to decide among them by itself.

important_terms.definition: The view that every concrete existent is either fundamentally a countable object or reducible to such objects.
A metaphysical category for material, and sometimes abstract, substance considered independently of individual objects.
A concrete entity that can be counted as one without using a measure, container, or partitive phrase.
A formal approach to parts and wholes. A fusion or sum is a whole composed of specified parts.
A composite object whose existence depends only on its ultimate parts, without requiring cohesion or functional unity.
The thesis that a mass of matter cannot survive the loss or replacement of any of its parts.
The linguistic contrast between expressions such as “water” and expressions such as “three horses,” though the contrast is disputed and context-sensitive.
A view that mass expressions refer to many objects together rather than to one sum or set.

questions_to_think_about: If two separated portions of water are still water, must they compose one larger thing?
Could a set of particles be identical with a concrete portion of gold, given that sets are often regarded as abstract?
Does referring to many particles require a further entity, such as a sum or plurality?
If mass/count grammar varies across languages, how much metaphysics can be inferred from English?
What should count as more fundamental: an ordinary object, its matter, or neither?

summaries.example: Suppose a smoothie is poured into two cups. You might say there is still the same smoothie, even though its parts are now separated. But if two bicycles are placed side by side, you would not normally say they make one bicycle. This difference suggests that some nouns describe stuff, while others describe countable things. A philosopher might explain the smoothie as one large sum of tiny parts, as many parts spoken of together, or as a kind of stuff that is not just another object.
summaries.summary: The entry explores a common but difficult distinction between stuff and things. We count things such as dogs, rocks, and bicycles, while we measure or portion stuff such as water, iron, and sand. This difference appears in language through mass expressions and count expressions. Philosophers use it to ask what mass expressions refer to and what the world is fundamentally made of. One family of views keeps Thing Theory and explains stuff as sums of particles or portions. Another treats stuff as sets of material parts. A third uses plural reference: “the water” may refer to many water-parts without naming one additional object. Other philosophers argue that stuff is not reducible to things and may be fundamental, while ordinary objects are dependent on it or are shaped by our ways of describing the world. The entry also examines problems for every approach, including matter that may be endlessly divisible and the fact that an object can change parts while the matter associated with it follows a different history. Its broader conclusion is that the mass/count distinction is useful evidence, but it is not obviously universal or fixed. Context can change how a word works, and different languages classify similar realities differently.
key_ideas: Stuff and things differ in how we usually talk about, measure, and count them.
Philosophers disagree about whether stuff is reducible to objects or is a basic part of reality.
A mereological theory treats a portion of stuff as a whole made from smaller parts.
A set theory treats stuff as a set of material pieces, while a plural theory refers to many pieces directly.
The stuff/thing distinction is connected to, but not identical with, the mass/count distinction in language.
Because words can change use and languages differ, grammar alone may not reveal the structure of reality.
summaries.why_it_matters: The subject helps explain why ordinary cases—such as water being poured, a tree being cut down, or metal making up a statue—raise deep questions about identity and existence. It also models philosophical disagreement: several theories can begin with the same observations yet interpret them differently. Finally, it encourages careful reasoning about the limits of language when making claims about the world.

important_terms.definition: A substance or material that is commonly measured or divided into portions rather than counted directly, such as water or iron.
An individual concrete object that can be counted as one, such as a bicycle, tree, or dog.
A word or phrase used with a mass meaning, such as “water,” “some sand,” or “the gold in the ring.”
A word or phrase used with a count meaning, such as “two bicycles” or “each tree.”
A theory saying that everything that exists is a thing or can be reduced to things.
The study of how parts combine into wholes.
A whole made from parts; in some theories, a sum may exist even when its parts are far apart.
A reference to several objects together, without necessarily treating them as one extra object.

questions_to_think_about: When two portions of water are poured together, is there one new thing or one larger portion of stuff?
Would identifying gold with a set of gold particles make gold abstract rather than physical?
Can “the furniture” refer to several chairs and tables without referring to one furniture-object?
Why might a philosopher think ordinary objects and their matter have different rules for surviving change?
Should a theory of reality depend heavily on the grammar of one language?
